title: InSight-o3: Empowering Multimodal Foundation Models with Generalized Visual Search
one_liner: Give a reasoning agent a dedicated visual search partner that can find the exact image regions described by a free-form request, even when the request names relations or concepts instead of simple objects.
lead: Many image-question systems can answer when the needed evidence sits in one obvious region. They struggle when the answer depends on several small regions spread across a chart, map, or document page. In those cases the hard part is not only reasoning. It is finding the right places to inspect. InSight-o3 splits the job between a reasoning agent and a visual search agent. The search agent is trained to locate regions described in free-form language, including relational requests such as "the legend entry that matches the steepest curve" or conceptual requests such as "the paragraph that states the exception." That extra search tool helps because the reasoning agent can only reason over details it has first brought into view.

problem.h2: Why hard image questions fail before reasoning starts
paras: A hard visual reasoning question often depends on several pieces of evidence in different places. For example, a chart question may require reading the legend, then matching a curve, then checking a value on the axis. A map question may require finding a symbol, reading a label far away, and comparing two routes.

A single agent that looks at the whole image at once often misses one of those details. Once an important detail is missed, later reasoning cannot recover it. The system needs a way to search for the exact region described by language before trying to combine those findings into an answer.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Separate visual search from reasoning, and train the search agent to localize free-form region descriptions so the reasoning agent can ask for the precise evidence it needs.

steps.b: Receive an image and a hard question.
steps.text: Start with a page, chart, map, or other dense image whose answer may depend on several distant regions.
The reasoning agent asks for a region in plain language, such as a curve segment, a legend item, or a sentence that states a condition.
The visual search agent finds the region that best matches the request, because it has been trained to handle free-form descriptions rather than only fixed object names.
Pass the found crop or coordinates back so the reasoning agent can read or compare the relevant content.

steps.b: Repeat until enough evidence is gathered.
steps.text: Ask for more regions as needed, then answer the question once the required details have been collected.

paras: The paper changes multimodal reasoning from one-agent whole-image inspection to a two-agent system in which one component specializes in visual search.
object.object: how the agent gathers visual evidence

hidden.name: Whether the needed visual evidence can be found from language alone
paras: A reasoning system fails if the evidence it needs is present in the image but never becomes accessible to the reasoning process. The hidden quantity is evidence reachability: can the agent actually bring the right region into view when the question describes it in ordinary language?

InSight-o3 raises evidence reachability by training a dedicated search agent to map free-form requests to image regions. This matters because many benchmark failures are not pure reasoning failures. They start as evidence-gathering failures.

heat.caption: Dark cells mark situations where the answer exists in the image but is hard to retrieve without a dedicated search skill.

reads.html: The agent must be able to fetch the right part of the image before reasoning about that part can help, because missing evidence cannot be repaired by later reasoning.
Generalized visual search improves evidence reachability because a specialized search agent learns to localize relational, fuzzy, and conceptual region requests.

mechanism.h2: Why splitting search from reasoning helps
paras: The method works because search and reasoning are different jobs. Search asks where the relevant evidence lives. Reasoning asks how several pieces of evidence combine into an answer. A single agent that tries to do both from the full image can waste effort scanning irrelevant content and still miss a small necessary detail.

Once the search agent becomes good at localizing free-form requests, the reasoning agent can operate on a cleaner evidence stream. Accuracy rises because each query narrows the visual field to what matters, and harder multi-region questions become manageable because the system can gather evidence step by step.

stages.s: Reasoner asks for a described region
Answer after enough evidence is gathered

math.words: For each search request, score candidate regions by how well the region matches the language description, then return the highest-scoring region to the reasoning agent.
symbols: the image region returned to the reasoning agent
a score that measures how well one region fits the free-form request
the language description of the needed evidence
a candidate crop or location in the image

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the question asks which line on a chart drops fastest after a certain date.
The reasoning agent first asks for the legend item tied to the darkest line.
The search agent scores several small legend regions and returns the best one.
Next the reasoning agent asks for the matching curve section after the date marker.
The search agent returns that curve region, and the reasoning agent compares the slopes.
The answer is now reachable because the evidence was collected in the right order.

math.note: The search score is useful because the reasoning agent does not need the whole image at once. It needs the best next region for the current subquestion.

bars.h2: What the result should look like

charts.title: Whole-image reasoning alone
charts.note: A single-agent system often misses small but necessary regions because it lacks a dedicated search stage.

charts.title: Reasoner plus visual search agent
charts.note: The added search agent helps because the reasoner can request and inspect the exact visual evidence needed for each step.

items.b: The search request may be underspecified.
items.html: If the reasoner asks for a vague region, the search agent may return the wrong crop because several places satisfy the request equally well.

items.b: The search agent may miss conceptual cues.
items.html: Some requests point to a function rather than a visible object, such as the sentence that states an exception. Those cases remain hard because the region is defined by meaning, not just appearance.
A long chain of search requests may add latency because each reasoning step waits for another localization pass.
When the reasoner asks precise subquestions and the search agent returns accurate crops, hard image questions become more solvable because the system can gather evidence in pieces.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Use a dense set of charts, maps, and document pages whose questions require several distant details. Compare a single multimodal reasoner against a two-agent setup with a visual search component. Log the intermediate search requests, the returned regions, and the final answers. The demo should show that the two-agent system answers more questions correctly because it can retrieve the needed evidence step by step instead of trying to reason over the whole page at once.
demo.closing: The main proof is that better visual evidence gathering leads to better final reasoning on dense images because the answer depends on details the reasoner must first bring into view.
